newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian debt yields slashed again on weak data.
newsitem.headline: Australian debt yields slashed again on weak data.

text.p: *Australian 10-year bond yields fell to their lowest level in 3-1/2 years after the June labour report showed only a small rise in total employment and a further drop in full-time jobs.
*Market on red alert for a monetary policy easing.

A much weaker than expected Australian employment report saw 10-year bond yields sink to their lowest level in some 3-1/2 year and the spread to the U.S. crushed to a point not seen in well over a decade.
September bill futures also rallied to a contract high of 94.99 with the market fully anticipating a 50 basis point easing at any time in the coming weeks, analysts said.
Total employment rose just 11,900 when expectations had been for a much stronger rebound after May's 40,300 slump, while full-time jobs fell a further 16,900.

And while the government took to heart a fall in the unemployment rate to 8.5 percent, this was largely due to less people looking for working with the participation rate dropping to 63.0 percent, or as UBS's chief economist Stephen Roberts put it, the "discouraged worker effect".

"For bonds it was much more bullish than expected. Given that we have got inflation data coming up in a couple of weeks and that looks very, very benign, the issue is when are they (the RBA) going to ease, and I think that you keep watching the screens," he added.

The data helped to push along the long-end's rally, which has now seen 10-year yields drop some 1-1/2 full points since early April and to well below 6.75 percent, while the spread to the U.S. shrank to under 40 basis points.

This yield differential has steadily dropped from 100 basis points in mid-May taking into account the last official rate cut on May 23, the recent positive credit rating outlook by Moody's and uncertainty over whether the Fed will have to tighten again. "The fantasy of Australia having lower yields across the curve than the U.S. might just be around the corner," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.

The short end, which has had a negative spread to the U.S. since just after the May 23 official rate cut to 5.5 percent, is nearing the minus 50 basis point level seen after the May jobs report. The market also outperformed Canada, but lost ground to New Zealand after its NZ$150 million auction of 2009 bonds.
